A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CREAM research, with matching authors, core algorithm and original experiments. Text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and can be matched across the expanded and reorganized material.

before.justification: v1 reports original Llama-2/Llama-3 benchmark experiments, preference-ranking evaluations, consistency analyses and ablations in Section 4 and Appendix B.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds comparator, longer-training, model-configuration and regularization experiments in Section 4 and Appendix C.

M1.justification: The default algorithm, intrinsic rewards and consistency-weighted normal/reversed DPO objective remain unchanged. Appendix C adds limited procedural variants: threshold-dependent regularization, per-example consistency weights and prompt-rewarding P-CREAM. The corrected worst-response selection formula agrees with v1's existing best/worst-response description.

E1.justification: Both versions use OpenAssistant, ARC-Easy/Challenge, OpenBookQA, SIQA and GSM8K, plus curated preference-ranking data and RewardBench. The added larger and initially unaligned models are configurations evaluated on retained tasks, without new datasets, domains or input scenarios.

E2.justification: v3 substantially expands evaluated comparators. Table 1 adds SRLM + KL and CREAM w/o RC; Tables 6, 8 and 12 add weighted-DPO SRLM, Ensemble-Worst, Ensemble-Mean, Distilled DPO and P-CREAM comparisons. Original SRLM, Oracle and P-SRLM comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: New protocols extend training from M3 through M6, evaluate Llama-2-13B and non-chat Llama-3-8B, and introduce regularization grids and three-model ensembles trained with different learning rates. Appendix C.2 also specifies checkpoint selection for weighted-DPO experiments. The original benchmark settings remain; newly specifying five responses per prompt is disclosure, not evidence of a changed sampling budget.

E4.justification: v3 adds targeted tests of adaptive versus fixed consistency, simple loss weighting, ensemble rewards, thresholded versus per-example regularization, and prompt-based regularization. It also examines M4–M6 stability, consistency distributions, model size and initial alignment. The original date-arithmetic case study in Section 4.3.4 and Table 5 is removed rather than relocated.

E5.justification: The existing plus/minus reporting in Table 2 is unchanged. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. New consistency-score distributions in Table 7 describe an additional analysis, without introducing a new uncertainty-estimation procedure for benchmark performance.

E6.justification: Original benchmark scores and Figures 3–5 are retained, and v1 Table 6 reappears as v3 Table 13. Extensive new results include CREAM's average peaking at 83.65 at M4 and declining to 82.73 at M6, versus SRLM's 68.59 at M6 (Table 5). New M3 comparisons report 57.46 versus 49.33 on Llama-2-13B and 42.67 versus 35.55 with initially unaligned Llama-3. These are added settings, not improvements to the original scores.

T1.justification: The original theorems, lemmas and proofs are retained, with Appendix A becoming B. Equations 3.11–3.12 correct worst-response selection from argmin to argmax. Appendices C.2 and C.4 add gradient/equal-ratio analysis, a zero-loss self-distillation minimizer argument and mathematical comparisons of regularization objectives; these supplement the existing theoretical framework.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: a generalized iterative preference framework, overconfident labeling as a source of rewarding bias, and cross-iteration consistency regularization to improve self-rewarding. Additional experiments support these claims without materially redefining their scope.

C2.justification: New discussion explains label smoothing versus loss scaling, the rarity of near-zero consistency, model-level uncertainty, and averaging as variance reduction. Appendices A and C.6 explicitly discuss computational costs and the need for initial alignment. Longer-term stability and ensemble comparisons receive substantive interpretations. The arena discussion also newly mentions GPT-4o as an opponent, although Figure 3 still shows it only as judge.

D1.justification: v3 newly specifies five sampled responses per prompt, comparator hyperparameter grids, ensemble learning rates and weighted-DPO checkpoint selection. Conversely, it removes the NVIDIA A6000 hardware statement and explicit GPT-4o provenance of curated preference labels. The code link and principal optimizer, learning-rate and epoch disclosures remain unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 2 and Appendix C.4 substantially expand positioning against reward hacking, reward-model ensembles and robust preference optimization, including Coste, Eisenstein, Rame, Zhang and Fisch. New distillation references support that discussion. Two peripheral vision-language references are removed. The revision develops substantive distinctions about preference regularization, conservatism and ensemble costs.

P1.justification: The introduction and experimental discussion are edited and condensed, the case-study subsection is removed, and appendices are reorganized into Limitations, Proofs and subdivided Additional Results. The main five-section narrative and method exposition remain largely intact. The publication header changes from Preprint to ICLR 2025.

P2.justification: Table 1 gains comparator rows and an Average column and is substantially resized. Eight new appendix tables appear as Tables 5–12; the original case-study table is removed, while v1 Table 6 becomes Table 13. Existing figures are retained, but experiment-page table placement, sizing and text flow are substantially rearranged.

improvement.justification: Table 1 and Appendix C substantially strengthen validation by testing adaptive consistency against simpler regularization and weighting alternatives, examining later-iteration degradation, and probing model-size and initial-alignment dependence. These address important gaps in v1, while explicit limitations clarify applicability. Lost hardware and label-provenance details and unsupported GPT-4o-opponent wording are drawbacks; run-based uncertainty also remains unreported. The targeted validation gains outweigh these narrower weaknesses.
